read: full: abstract, sections 1-6 (pp. 1-10) in full; appendices A-C (writing aid, preliminary study, training, PLS worked example, manual annotation, mitigation details, pp. 18-19) read; remaining appendix figures and prompts skimmed
venue_now: ICLR 2026 (header on every page: 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026'; arXiv 2502.01534v3, 4 Mar 2026; first posted Feb 2025)
what_it_is: Defines 'preference leakage': when the LLM that generates synthetic training data and the LLM used as judge are related (the same model, an inheritance relation through fine-tuning or distillation, or the same model family), the judge favours student models trained on that data. Three generator/judge LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-flash, LLaMA-3.3-70B) each produce responses to 30,000 UltraFeedback prompts; pre-trained Mistral-7B and Qwen-2.5-14B are fine-tuned on each set, and the students are compared pairwise by each judge on Arena-Hard (500 questions) and AlpacaEval 2.0 (805). A preference leakage score (PLS) measures how much each judge favours its related student. Further analyses vary relatedness, student size, data mixing, learning method, question type and spurious features, test whether judges can recognise their students, and try mitigations.
domain: open-ended instruction following and chat (Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval 2.0); question types include mathematics, programming, science, writing, business and daily life
size: 3 generator/judge LLMs (plus GPT-4-turbo, Gemini-1.5-pro, GPT-3.5-turbo, Gemini-1.0-pro in the family analysis); 2 main student models (more sizes of LLaMA-3, Qwen-2.5, Qwen-3 in the size analysis); 30,000 synthetic training examples per generator; 500 + 805 evaluation questions
source_of_items: existing benchmarks (Arena-Hard, AlpacaEval 2.0); training data synthesised by the generator LLMs from UltraFeedback prompts
evaluation: LLM judge, pairwise win rates converted to a preference leakage score; for mitigation, an Error Bias metric against human-labelled pairwise judgments (PPE, MT-Bench, Chatbot Arena human preferences)
human_validation: Three annotators compared responses on 100 AlpacaEval 2.0 questions (average agreement 78.6) to check which judges are most biased (appendix C.3, p. 19); the mitigation study uses existing human-labelled preference data (p. 10). The judges themselves are not validated against expert correctness labels.
contamination_measures: not applicable (the paper treats judge-generator relatedness as a form of contamination; it does not protect its own benchmarks)

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate, not cited in the May paper. It is the peer-reviewed basis for EngTrace's roster rule (D-110: no judge from a model family on the roster). The May Tribunal (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3) judged a roster containing the same models and their families, and open-weight models plausibly distilled from them: all three of this paper's relatedness types (pp. 3-4). Its Table 2 (p. 7) shows the score inflation is largest for the same model (PLS 23.6%) and inheritance (19.3-22.3%), smaller within a model family and series (8.9%), and small across series (2.8%). Two cautions for the revision. (1) Inheritance includes a judge trained on data from a generator (the relation is bidirectional, p. 4); MiMo-V2.5-Pro's documented exposure to Claude outputs, with Claude Sonnet 5 on the roster, is a case of that type, so the paper supports saying the judge is outside every roster family with a small, disclosed distillation exposure, not that it is unrelated. (2) Leakage was lowest for mathematics questions (PLS 7.7%, Figure 3a p. 9) and objective judgment dimensions, which is closer to EngTrace's milestone verdicts against gold values than to the chat setting where it was measured; and judges could not recognise their related students' outputs (Table 5, pp. 8-9), so detection has to come from outside validation, as EngTrace's expert labels provide.

suggested_wording: A judge related to the evaluated models, as the same model, through distillation or fine-tuning, or within the same family, inflates their scores in ways it cannot itself detect (Li et al., 2026); EngTrace's residual judge is therefore drawn from a family outside the evaluated roster, and its one documented distillation exposure is disclosed.
facts_to_cite: Defines preference leakage as judge bias caused by relatedness between the synthetic-data generator and the judge, with three relatedness types: same model, inheritance, same model family (abstract p. 1; section 3.3 pp. 3-4).

Main setup: GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-flash and LLaMA-3.3-70B generate 30,000 SFT examples each; Mistral-7B and Qwen-2.5-14B students are judged pairwise on Arena-Hard (500) and AlpacaEval 2.0 (805) (pp. 4-5).

Judges favour their related students in most model pairs, e.g. average PLS 23.6% (Mistral) and 27.9% (Qwen) for the GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5 pair, while the GPT-4o and LLaMA-3.3 pair is near zero (Table 1, pp. 5-6).
PLS by relatedness: same model 23.6%; inheritance 19.3% (same instructions) and 22.3% (different instructions); same family, same series 8.9%; same family, different series 2.8% (Table 2, p. 7).
Leakage grows with the share of related synthetic data, with no clear threshold, and is larger for smaller students (pp. 6-7).
SFT leaks most (23.6%), DPO less (5.2%), in-context learning not at all (-2.7%) (Table 3, pp. 7-8).

Judges cannot recognise their related students' outputs (accuracy 29.8%-53.2%), while a BERT classifier separates the students at 82.4%, so preference leakage is harder to detect than egocentric bias (Table 5, pp. 8-9).
Leakage is lowest for mathematics questions (PLS 7.7%) and highest for programming (31.4%), and lower on objective than subjective judgment dimensions (Figure 3, p. 9; conclusion p. 10).

Removing style and format from responses reduces leakage; contextual calibration reduces a human-anchored Error Bias from 17.8 to 7.3, while prompting and paraphrasing do not help (Tables 6-7, pp. 9-10).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: the concern that judge-candidate relatedness (same model, family, distillation) biases scores, which motivates EngTrace's out-of-roster residual judge; a human-anchored check of bias. Lacks: generated instances, gold traces, step-level evaluation, engineering or correctness-based tasks (pairwise chat preferences), and expert validation of the judge; it measures leakage through students trained on synthetic data, not a judge scoring its own or its family's outputs directly.
notes: Paragraph: process supervision and judge validity. Error in the paper: p. 9 says 'preference leakage tends to be more significant in objective questions and dimensions', which contradicts the results just reported (mathematics lowest) and the conclusion ('especially in subjective questions and judgment dimensions', p. 10); read it as 'subjective'. Small correction to the search note: MT-Bench is not one of the main evaluation tasks; it appears only in the preliminary survey (appendix B, p. 18) and as a source of human-labelled pairs for mitigation (p. 10). Key it by venue year (2026); the brief's 'Li et al. 2025' is the arXiv year. The paper's own setting (chat preferences, judges scoring SFT students) is far from EngTrace's, so cite it for the relatedness taxonomy and the direction of the effect, not for magnitudes. For the writers: evaluator_pilot_17092026/JUDGE_SELECTION.md (line 54) says 'Distillation exposure is weaker than shared family'; this paper does not support that ordering, since in its setup inheritance (PLS 19.3-22.3%) exceeds same family (8.9% same series, 2.8% different series) (Table 2, p. 7). What it does support is that leakage scales with the share of related synthetic data and 'can occur even with a small amount' (Figure 2b p. 6; text p. 7), so the case for MiMo should rest on the small size of its documented exposure (0.4M Claude exchanges, the smallest named, per JUDGE_SELECTION.md), which predicts a smaller but not a zero effect, and on the expert validation, not on distillation being a weaker kind of relatedness.
